name: Will to power
plain_explanation: Nietzsche holds that the deepest drive in human beings -- more fundamental than pleasure, self-preservation, or even truth-seeking -- is the desire for power, for the capacity to overcome resistance, endure hardship, and impose one's will on the world and on others.
precise_definition: Nietzsche's central psychological and ethical category: the drive to power as the fundamental measure of vitality and worth, tested (per Nietzsche's own words quoted by Russell) 'according to the amount of resistance it can offer and the amount of pain and torture it can endure and know how to turn to its own advantage.'
why_it_mattered: It grounds Nietzsche's entire revaluation of values: strength, cruelty, discipline, and the capacity to inflict and endure suffering become goods, while compassion and equality become symptoms of weakness to be overcome.
historical_origin: Developed across Nietzsche's mature works, especially Beyond Good and Evil and The Will to Power.
examples: 'I do not point to the evil and pain of existence with the finger of reproach, but rather entertain the hope that life may one day become more evil and more full of suffering than it has ever been.'
Nietzsche's hope for 'a new vast aristocracy based upon the most severe self-discipline, in which the will of philosophical men of power and artist-tyrants will be stamped upon thousands of years.'
objections: Russell argues the lust for power Nietzsche endows his superman with is itself, unrecognized by Nietzsche, an outcome of fear: 'those who do not fear their neighbours see no necessity to tyrannize over them.'
competing_positions: Schopenhauer's will, which is metaphysically fundamental but ethically evil, to be renounced rather than affirmed
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became one of Nietzsche's most widely (and, Russell implies, sometimes crudely) influential ideas among artistic and literary, rather than technical-philosophical, audiences.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly opposed to Christian ethics, which Nietzsche sees as suppressing the will to power in favor of 'slave morality.'
